paras: The Manitou streetcar mob threat against William Johnson took place on August 14, 1910, when a crowd of nearly 500 surrounded Johnson, a Black porter of Colorado Springs, at the end of the car line in Manitou, Colorado, after he was accused of insolence to a white woman over a seat. Police removed him to the county jail, and four days later a jury fined him $1 and costs after the evidence failed to show insolence. The Denver Star used the case to attack the white daily press for its eagerness to report a lynching over streetcar manners.

Johnson was a porter who lived in Colorado Springs, and the Denver Star described him and Connell as young men well known in Denver and living in Colorado Springs. The incident took place on a Sunday at the end of the street-car line in Manitou, where tourists as well as residents were present.

According to the Colorado Springs wire report, Johnson boarded the car and tried to hold a double seat, and a Denver woman named as Mrs. Peterson sat down beside him without intending to. The same report said that a moment later Johnson pushed her off the seat so that she fell to the floor of the car. The white passengers were then 'in an uproar,' several 'advised lynching,' and nearly 500 'excited tourists and residents' surrounded Johnson.

Police arrived and, with difficulty, took Johnson away to a cell in the county jail. A second dispatch the next day said that Johnson and another Black man, Alva Cornell, had both been 'rescued from a mob' that afternoon.

Johnson and Cornell were held for trial on charges of assault and of resisting an officer. On August 18 a jury at Colorado Springs fined Johnson $1 and costs, and a dispatch reported that 'the evidence failed' to prove he had been insolent to Mrs. Peterson. No report of Cornell's trial or of any action against members of the crowd appears in the coverage.

The first wire story ran on August 15 in the Albuquerque Morning Journal under 'Insolent Porter Has Narrow Escape,' in the Los Angeles Herald, and in the Salt Lake Herald-Republican under 'Lynching Was Averted.' These reports gave the accusation as fact and offered no account from Johnson. A shorter follow-up, which said Johnson 'had insulted a white woman,' appeared in the San Francisco Call and the Los Angeles Herald on August 16 and in an Idaho weekly's 'Northwest Notes' on August 26.

The Denver Star answered on August 20 with an editorial saying that 'no offense was intended nor any taken' and that 'outside interference and misunderstanding' had caused the bitterness. Its editor wrote that it was 'wonderful on what small pretext that lust for blood of Negroes rises' and asked what should be said of a white press that was 'such a willing ally' of the mob. The editorial then urged readers to weigh what they received for their money from the white dailies against what they got from race papers. The Star's Denver news column added that Alva Connell and Willie Johnson, 'young men well known in Denver,' were nearly lynched for seeking 'the self-respect due their wives.' A week later the Colorado Statesman printed the dispatch on Johnson's $1 fine.

The white wire said Johnson pushed Mrs. Peterson from a seat she had taken unintentionally, while the Denver Star said the white woman started the trouble by trying to force a seat from Johnson after he had occupied it. The trial dispatch said he was alleged to have pushed her to make room for his female companion, and the jury's verdict did not sustain the charge of insolence. Accounts also differ on the woman's name, given as Mrs. Alfred Peterson, Mrs. Marie Peters and Mrs. J. Peterson, and on the second man's surname, Cornell or Connell.

reader.title: Manitou streetcar mob threat against William Johnson
bases: A crowd of nearly 500 surrounded a Black man accused of insolence to a white woman and several 'advised lynching' before police removed him (A3, A4, A5); no one was killed, so this is a threatened lynching.

No one was killed: police removed Johnson to the county jail and he was later tried and fined (A4, A6, A12). The crowd of nearly 500 acted without authority on a charge of insolence to a white woman (A4, A5), so it was a lynching threat, not a lynching.

The white wire reports (A3, A4, A6) and two independent Black-press sources, the Denver Star (A8, A9) and the Colorado Statesman's dispatch (A12), agree that Johnson was nearly lynched at Manitou after a streetcar seat dispute, though they disagree over who was at fault.

framing.detail: The wire called Johnson an 'insolent porter' and gave his pushing of the woman as fact, with no version from Johnson.
The follow-up stated as fact that Johnson 'had insulted a white woman' and reported the two men held for trial.
The Denver Star wrote of the 'lust for blood of Negroes' rising on 'small pretext' and called the white press a 'willing ally' of the mob's conduct.
The Colorado Statesman ran a short dispatch on the trial noting that insolence was not proved.
